title: He will crush your head
teaser: The first promise of the Gospel, hidden inside a curse, and the long road from Eden to the empty tomb.

panels.heading: WHEN THE FIRST GOOD NEWS COMES
panels.content:
Take a breath here. We are still on the third page of the Bible, and the world is already broken. Adam has hidden. Eve has hidden. The ground will start to push back against the hands that work it. A relationship that was naked and unashamed has put on the first clothing made of blame.

And into that wreckage, God speaks. Not first to the man. Not first to the woman. He turns to the serpent and says something stranger than a punishment. He makes a promise. The very first promise on the lips of God after the fall is not a sentence written against us. It is a sentence written for us. Listen for it.

panels.heading: THE PROMISE INSIDE THE CURSE
panels.content:
Here is what God says to the serpent in the BSB:

**"And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed; He will crush your head, and you will strike His heel."** (Genesis 3:15)

Readers since the second century have called this verse the *protoevangelium*: the first announcement of the Good News. The Gospel before the Gospel. It arrives early, embedded in a curse spoken over the snake, but its center of gravity points all the way forward to a Cross.

The ancient Near East heard cosmic-combat stories like this all the time. The hero gods of Babylon and Canaan crushed serpentine chaos to bring order. Genesis takes that grammar and rewrites it. The serpent is not a rival deity; he is a creature. The hero is not a god of the storm; He is a man, born of a woman, who will take a wound to His heel in order to break the head of the one who hates us.

Jewish readers heard the same hint. The Aramaic Targum Onkelos, paraphrasing the Hebrew for synagogue use centuries before Jesus, already read the woman's seed as a coming Messianic figure. Hebrew Scripture was already leaning forward, even when it did not know His name.

panels.heading: THE SEED, THE SERPENT, AND THE CROSS
panels.content:
Pay attention to one Hebrew detail. The word for "seed," *zera*, is a collective noun. It can mean an entire line of descendants, or one specific descendant. Genesis 3:15 leaves the door open. Paul walks straight through it. Writing to the Galatians, he insists the promises were spoken "to Abraham and to his seed... that is, Christ" (Galatians 3:16). Then, a chapter later: "when the fullness of time had come, God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the Law" (Galatians 4:4). The serpent is told there will be a Seed. The Apostle tells us who.

The early church saw this clearly. Irenaeus, writing around 180 AD, called this verse the very beginning of the Gospel and read the head-crushing as the work of Christ on the Cross. The bruised heel ends the serpent's reign. Justin Martyr made the same connection a generation earlier. Calvin would later write, "Although in the whole human race Christ alone is the head, yet the apostle teaches that all the godly are partakers of this victory."

Which is why Paul, near the end of Romans, lifts his eyes and says, "The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet" (Romans 16:20). The head-crushing began at Calvary. It is still finishing in us. It will be complete when He returns. One promise, three movements: announced in Eden, accomplished on the Cross, completed at His coming.

panels.heading: A GOSPEL FOR YOUR ACTUAL DAY
panels.content:
Sit with this for a minute, because it changes how you read the rest of your Bible, and how you read your own life.

The Good News is not something God came up with later, after a Plan A had failed. The Good News was already loaded into the first sentence God spoke after the fall. Before there was a Law, before there was a temple, before there was a king, there was a promise: a Seed, a wound, a crushed head.

Which means the next time you find yourself reading a hard chapter, a flood, a wandering tribe, a long stretch of failed kings, you are not reading a record of God's frustration. You are reading the slow, patient unfolding of a promise He made on the worst day in human history. He has been keeping it ever since.

panels.heading: A PRAYER FOR EYES TO SEE
panels.content: Father, give me eyes to see the Gospel even where I expect a curse. Teach me that Your first word after my fall was a promise, not a verdict. Where the serpent still hisses in my thoughts today (accusation, shame, despair), let me hear instead the older voice of Eden: a Seed is coming, and His heel has already done the work. Crush what hates me. Keep what loves me. In the name of Jesus, the long-promised Seed of the woman. Amen.

sources: Irenaeus of Lyon. *Against Heresies*, Book III, Chapter 23 (c. 180 AD). Earliest sustained reading of Genesis 3:15 as the protoevangelium fulfilled in Christ.
John Calvin. *Commentaries on the Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Romans*, on Romans 16:20 (1540). On the church's participation in Christ's victory over the serpent.
